summary_html: An intake **screen** is elevated to a formal **investigation/assessment** under state criteria. CAPTA and CFSR establish the federal expectations for screening, timelines, and investigative quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening/investigation conditions for funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review framework

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: A social worker and police officer may enter a home without a warrant to check on children reported abused only if the officer is actually motivated by a need to render aid and, objectively, a reasonable person would have believed an emergency existed.
key_cases.relevance: It marks the constitutional line an intake screen must clear before workers enter a family's home.
key_cases.quote: Both tests must be satisfied before a warrantless entry will be justified under the emergency rule exception.

key_cases.holding: Wisconsin recognizes no damages claim against caseworkers for intentional interference with 'family unity,' and in any event county social workers are immune for discretionary acts; conclusory allegations of malice do not pierce that immunity.
key_cases.relevance: Decisions to escalate or not escalate an intake are discretionary acts shielded from damages suits.
key_cases.quote: public officers and employees enjoy immunity from suit for discretionary actions undertaken in the scope of their public employment

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: Wisconsin caseworkers violated the Fourth Amendment and the plaintiffs' right to familial relations by entering a private school and seizing and interviewing a child without a warrant, court order, probable cause, exigent circumstances, or parental or school consent.
key_cases.relevance: Escalating a screened report to an on-site child interview is itself a Fourth Amendment seizure requiring justification.
key_cases.quote: Thus, although child welfare caseworkers may investigate allegations of child abuse without violating parents' constitutional right to familial relations, they may not do so arbitrarily.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: A caseworker's visual examination of a child's body during a child-abuse investigation is a search within the Fourth Amendment, but neither a warrant nor probable cause is required; its constitutionality turns on contextual reasonableness, which this preliminary record could not resolve, so the denial of an injunction and the individual defendants' qualified immunity were affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Escalating a hotline report to an on-site examination of a child is a search whose reasonableness must be justified by more than the screening criteria themselves.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, whether a search is "reasonable," in the constitutional sense, will vary according to the context of the search.

state_agency.name: Wisconsin Department of Children and Families
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the county or tribal agency where the child lives — the list is at dcf.wisconsin.gov/reportabuse

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, naturopathic doctors, nurses, dentists, chiropractors, optometrists, acupuncturists, and medical or mental health professionals not otherwise specified (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)1., 1m., 4.–9.)
Social workers, marriage and family therapists, and professional counselors (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)10.–12.)
Public assistance workers, including financial and employment planners (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)13.)
School teachers, school administrators, school counselors, and school employees not otherwise specified (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)14.–16., 16m.)
Child care workers in a child care center, group home, or residential care center for children and youth, and child care providers (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)18., 19.)
Alcohol or other drug abuse counselors and genetic counselors (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)20., 20m.)

Treatment staff employed by or working under contract with a county department under Wis. Stat. § 46.23, 51.42, or 51.437, or with a residential care center for children and youth (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)21.)
Physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, occupational therapists, and dietitians (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)22., 22m., 23., 24.)
Emergency medical services practitioners and emergency medical responders (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)27., 28.)
Police or law enforcement officers and juvenile correctional officers (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(a)29., 30.)
Court-appointed special advocates, as to children seen in the course of activities under Wis. Stat. § 48.236(3) (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(b))
Members of the clergy, except for child abuse information received solely through confidential communications made privately or in a confessional setting (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(bm)1.–3.)
Any other person, including an attorney — permissive only; may report but is not required to (Wis. Stat. § 48.981(2)(c))

notice_requirements.timing: Within 24 hours after a county department that has a federally recognized reservation or the Ho-Chunk service area wholly or partly within its county receives a report about a child it knows or has reason to know is an Indian child residing in the county, or an Indian unborn child whose expectant mother resides in the county
content_required: Name and address of the Indian child or expectant mother
The fact that a report has been received about that Indian child or Indian unborn child

statutory_basis.citation_text: Wis. Stat. § 48.981(3)(bm) (notice of report to Indian tribal agent)
